# Part 1: The AI Foundry Constitution

We seek to establish a world-class culture. Following Brigham Young's admonition to gather up all
the good and true principles wherever we find them, hence we've draw inspiration from many places including:

- [BYU Marriott School of Business, Vision, Mission, and Values](https://marriott.byu.edu/our-story/mission/)
- [The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, the standard works](https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/scriptures?lang=eng)
- [The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, Christlike Attributes, Preach My Gospel, Chapter 6](https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/manual/preach-my-gospel-2023/14-chapter-6?lang=eng)
- [Amazon, Leadership Principles](https://www.amazon.jobs/content/en/our-workplace/leadership-principles)
- [Bridgewater, Original Philosophy](https://www.bridgewater.com/culture/bridgewaters-original-philosophy)
- [McKinsey, Purpose, Mission, and Values](https://www.mckinsey.com/about-us/overview/our-purpose-mission-and-values)
- [John Wooden, The Pyramid of Success](https://coachwooden.com/pyramid-of-success)
- [Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II](https://classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/nicomachaen.2.ii.html)

## Our principles

List of values often list principles to be maximized such as: be excellent, be truthful, be bold. Such lists are helpful but often suffer from two limitations.

1) Almost any good quality can be taken to excess. Excellence can overshoot into perfectionism.
Boldness can overshoot into recklessness. A simple list of values usually provides no way to acknowledge "it's possible to do too much of a good thing."

2) Two good principles may collide with each. Speed collides with rigor. Candor collides
with kindness. Excellence collides with a deadline.

Fortunately, Aristotle elegantly solved both limitations by using a concept he called the Golden Mean. The character traits we seek often sit between two failure modes: doing too little or doing too much. Courage is not the opposite of cowardice; it sits as a Golden Mean, that is, a weighted average, between cowardice and recklessness. Generosity sits between stinginess and waste.

Aristotle was clear that the Golden Mean is not fixed by a formula but rather found by good judgment, and
good judgment comes from reflecting on real experience, either your own or that of others.

Aristotle called these qualities virtues. We call them principles, which is more modern language
for the same concept. Each of the fourteen below is written with possible failure modes named.

These principles are aspirational and we may frequently miss Golden Mean. Yet we keep
striving, and over time develop true wisdom and good judgement.

We are successful when we can honestly say this of ourselves:

> "Success is peace of mind which is a direct result of self-satisfaction in knowing you made the
> effort to become the best of which you are capable."
>
> John Wooden

## Our four commitments

### 1. Seek truth, and use it well^1^

| Principle | Too little | The golden mean | Too much |
|---|---|---|---|
| Act with integrity^2^ | Deceitful | States it plainly, including the part that costs something | Self-righteous |
| Be discerning^3^ | Repeats what was said in confidence. Says the true thing that only wounds | Tells the person who needs it, in the way they can receive it | Calls it discretion when it is avoidance |
| Be courageous^4^ | Goes along | Challenges, then commits | Fights for ego |

### 2. Think hard and stay teachable^5^

| Principle | Too little | The golden mean | Too much |
|---|---|---|---|
| Be curious^6^ | Accepts the brief as given. Stops at the first answer | Asks the question behind the question | Chases the interesting question instead of the one that matters |
| Be rigorous^7^ | Accepts what sounds right. Trusts the output without checking the reasoning | Reasons from first principles | Rederives what is already settled. Demands proof past the point the decision needs |
| Choose humility^8^ | Defends the position instead of testing it. Ties ego to being right | Asks what they missed, then changes | Hedges. Defers when they know better |
| Seek personal improvement^9^ | Hears the feedback and files it | Asks for the critique, then acts on it | Works on themselves instead of the work. Makes every review about their growth |

### 3. Do great work^10^

| Principle | Too little | The golden mean | Too much |
|---|---|---|---|
| Act in faith^11^ | Waits for certainty. Needs the risk gone before starting | Moves on incomplete information | Skips the preparation and calls it faith |
| Strive for excellence^12^ | Settles for what passes. Mistakes activity for achievement | Raises the bar, then clears it | Polishes past the point of value. Wields the standard to shame |
| Demonstrate high agency^13^ | Waits to be told. Explains why it was not theirs | Sees the gap and closes it | Takes what was not theirs to take. Carries it alone instead of raising it |
| Show patience^14^ | Forces the answer before it is ready. Quits when it gets hard | Presses where it can move, waits where it cannot | Waits and calls it patience. Tolerates what should have been escalated |

### 4. Make each other better^15^

| Principle | Too little | The golden mean | Too much |
|---|---|---|---|
| Respect others^16^ | Talks past people. Dismisses the junior voice | Listens before answering | Trades candor for comfort. Plays favorites |
| Forgive quickly^17^ | Keeps score. Lets it color the next interaction | Says it once, then lets it go | Forgives before anything is named, so the pattern repeats |
| Develop others^18^ | Keeps what they know. Treats a teammate as a pair of hands | Hands it over and explains the why | Does it for them instead of with them |

## When there is no golden mean

Aristotle is explicit that the idea of the golden mean has limits: some thing "imply by their
names that they are themselves bad," and of those "it is not possible, then, ever to be right with
regard to them." 

## Sometimes principles collide

They will. Rigor says check it again; the deadline says ship. Courage says say it now; discernment
says not in this room, not in front of these people. Excellence says raise the bar; patience says
this is not the week.

Three things can be helpful when collision occur:

**Name the collision out loud.** "I think rigor and the deadline are fighting here" is a faster
route to a decision than arguing the merits as though only one principle were in play.

**Correct against your own pull.** Aristotle's coaching instruction is that aiming straight at the
golden mean undershoots, because your own habit is already bending you. Learn which way you
personally miss, then overcorrect. "We shall get into the intermediate state by drawing well away
from error, as people do in straightening sticks that are bent."

**The red face test.** When a situation is genuinely ambiguous, ask: could I explain this decision
to a respected leader without being red in the face? If not, do not do it.

# Part 2: AI Foundry Operating Model

## Flat hierarchy

Client teams operate without hierarchy. A team may be composed of 1 undergrad and 1 MBA, 2
undergrads, or 2 MBAs; in some cases teams may be slightly larger. In all cases, teams are flat
with no hierarchy. Every member of the team has equal accountability and equal authority. Degree
program, seniority, or AI Foundry leadership role confer no rank inside a team.

What this means in practice:

- **Self-organization.** Teams align on work streams themselves. They divide work by strength and
  interest, not by status.
- **Equal accountability.** The team owns the outcome together. If a deliverable slips or misses
  the bar, that belongs to everyone on the team.
- **Peer feedback.** Team members give feedback directly to each other as the first and normal
  channel.
- **Escalation.** When an issue cannot be resolved within the team, escalations go through JD and
  Scott.
- **Resetting teams.** If a team does not work well together it can be recomposed. This is a
  normal operating mechanism, not a punishment.

## Two courses, two roles

The AI Foundry is a cross-listed class with an undergraduate section (STRAT 490R) and a graduate
section (MBA 693R). For cross-listed courses, earning graduate credit is required to carry
requirements beyond the undergraduate expectations. In the AI Foundry, that requirement is met by
adding an organization leadership role: students in the graduate section help run the AI Foundry
itself.

- **Students in the undergraduate section build.** Their job is excellent client work, similar to
  Sandbox, except building for clients instead of for yourself.
- **Students in the graduate section build plus administer the organization itself.** They do the
  same client work, and in addition take on a leadership role in running the AI Foundry as an
  organization: operations, client pipeline, quality, recruiting, and culture.

::: {.callout-note}
With permission from the faculty advisor, undergraduates are eligible to enroll in the graduate
section and be considered for AI Foundry leadership roles.
:::

The two sections with associated roles for those enrolled in the graduate section does not violate
the flat hierarchy principle. Inside a client team, an MBA, or an undergraduate enrolled in the
graduate section, has no rank over a student enrolled in the undergraduate section. Every team
member has equal accountability and authority for the client work they are staffed to. The
leadership roles are a different responsibility expected only in the graduate course and do not
invoke any kind of authority over a teammate.

## The Ask First feedback culture

Everyone is empowered to give feedback to anyone at any time, respectfully and directly. More
important, our norm is to regularly **ask** for feedback. Asking removes the awkwardness of
unsolicited criticism, signals humility, and puts each of us in control of our own growth. A
practical habit: at the end of a project, a meeting, or a deliverable review, ask at least one
person "what is one thing I could have done better?" Feedback flows in every direction, including
to the faculty advisor. In general, teams should carve out 15 minutes for mutual feedback once
every two weeks.

The most useful version of that question, given how Part 1 is written, is directional: which way
did I miss? Too little or too much is a far easier thing for a teammate to answer than a rating,
and it is the only kind of answer you can act on.

## Amending this document

This document belongs to the whole team. Anyone may propose a change by raising it in a team
meeting or with the faculty advisor. We review proposed changes together and revisit the whole
document at the start of each semester so it stays alive rather than becoming wall art.

Because this page is the binding version and members sign against it, it changes by amendment
rather than by direct edit. When a change is agreed, the faculty advisor updates this page and the
date at the top reflects the version in force.
